claim: Sensory integration difficulties have been reported in autism.
source: Sensory integration difficulties have been reported in autism, but their underlying brain-circuit mechanisms are underexplored.
evidence: This is a general statement about autism that is supported by the context of the manuscript and the research it presents.

claim: The underlying brain-circuit mechanisms of sensory integration difficulties in autism are underexplored.
source: Sensory integration difficulties have been reported in autism, but their underlying brain-circuit mechanisms are underexplored.
evidence: This statement is presented as a motivation for the study.

claim: Delay eyeblink conditioning is a form of associative sensory learning requiring cerebellar plasticity.
source: Using five autism-related mouse models, Shank3+/ΔC, Mecp2R308/Y, Cntnap2−/−, L7-Tsc1 (L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+), and patDp(15q11-13)/+, we report specific perturbations in delay eyeblink conditioning, a form of associative sensory learning requiring cerebellar plasticity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about delay eyeblink conditioning.

claim: Response probability was reduced in Cntnap2−/− mice.
source: By distinguishing perturbations in the probability and characteristics of learned responses, we found that probability was reduced in Cntnap2−/−, patDp(15q11-13)/+, and L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+, which are associated with Purkinje-cell/deep-nuclear gene expression, along with Shank3+/ΔC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Response probability was reduced in patDp(15q11-13)/+ mice.
source: By distinguishing perturbations in the probability and characteristics of learned responses, we found that probability was reduced in Cntnap2−/−, patDp(15q11-13)/+, and L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+, which are associated with Purkinje-cell/deep-nuclear gene expression, along with Shank3+/ΔC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Response probability was reduced in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice.
source: By distinguishing perturbations in the probability and characteristics of learned responses, we found that probability was reduced in Cntnap2−/−, patDp(15q11-13)/+, and L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+, which are associated with Purkinje-cell/deep-nuclear gene expression, along with Shank3+/ΔC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cntnap2−/−, patDp(15q11-13)/+, and L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ are associated with Purkinje-cell/deep-nuclear gene expression.
source: By distinguishing perturbations in the probability and characteristics of learned responses, we found that probability was reduced in Cntnap2−/−, patDp(15q11-13)/+, and L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+, which are associated with Purkinje-cell/deep-nuclear gene expression, along with Shank3+/ΔC.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Response amplitudes were smaller in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice.
source: Amplitudes were smaller in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ as well as Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y, which are associated with granule cell pathway expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

source: Amplitudes were smaller in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ as well as Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y, which are associated with granule cell pathway expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Response amplitudes were smaller in Mecp2R308/Y mice.
source: Amplitudes were smaller in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ as well as Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y, which are associated with granule cell pathway expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y are associated with granule cell pathway expression.
source: Amplitudes were smaller in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ as well as Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y, which are associated with granule cell pathway expression.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Shank3+/ΔC mice showed aberrant response timing.
source: Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y also showed aberrant response timing and reduced Purkinje-cell dendritic spine density.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mecp2R308/Y mice showed aberrant response timing.
source: Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y also showed aberrant response timing and reduced Purkinje-cell dendritic spine density.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Shank3+/ΔC mice showed reduced Purkinje-cell dendritic spine density.

evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mecp2R308/Y mice showed reduced Purkinje-cell dendritic spine density.
source: Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y also showed aberrant response timing and reduced Purkinje-cell dendritic spine density.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The observations are potentially accounted for by defects in instructed learning in the olivocerebellar loop.
source: Overall, our observations are potentially accounted for by defects in instructed learning in the olivocerebellar loop and response representation in the granule cell pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on known cerebellar circuitry.

claim: The observations are potentially accounted for by defects in response representation in the granule cell pathway.
source: Overall, our observations are potentially accounted for by defects in instructed learning in the olivocerebellar loop and response representation in the granule cell pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on known cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Defects in associative temporal binding of sensory events are widespread in autism mouse models.
source: Our findings indicate that defects in associative temporal binding of sensory events are widespread in autism mouse models.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings across multiple mouse models.

claim: Atypical sensory processing is widely reported in autism starting in infancy.
source: In autism spectrum disorder (ASD; hereafter referred to as autism), atypical sensory processing is widely reported starting in infancy (Leekam et al., 2007; Markram and Markram, 2010; Dinstein et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Abnormal processing of single sensory modalities occurs in early life in autism.
source: In addition to early-life abnormal processing of single sensory modalities (Leekam et al., 2007), more complex deficits become apparent as early as 2 years of age, a time when autistic children attend poorly to natural combinations of spoken stimuli and natural visual motion (Klin et al., 2009), a circumstance that calls upon the ability to integrate, from moment to moment, information from two sensory modalities, hearing and vision.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: More complex sensory deficits become apparent as early as 2 years of age in autism.
source: In addition to early-life abnormal processing of single sensory modalities (Leekam et al., 2007), more complex deficits become apparent as early as 2 years of age, a time when autistic children attend poorly to natural combinations of spoken stimuli and natural visual motion (Klin et al., 2009), a circumstance that calls upon the ability to integrate, from moment to moment, information from two sensory modalities, hearing and vision.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Autistic children attend poorly to natural combinations of spoken stimuli and natural visual motion.
source: In addition to early-life abnormal processing of single sensory modalities (Leekam et al., 2007), more complex deficits become apparent as early as 2 years of age, a time when autistic children attend poorly to natural combinations of spoken stimuli and natural visual motion (Klin et al., 2009), a circumstance that calls upon the ability to integrate, from moment to moment, information from two sensory modalities, hearing and vision.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Abnormalities of sensory responsiveness are strongly correlated with severity of social phenotypes in high-functioning autism patients.
source: Abnormalities of sensory responsiveness are strongly correlated with severity of social phenotypes in high-functioning autism patients (Hilton et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Abnormal processing of multiple sensory modalities on subsecond time scales might impede the acquisition of cognitive and affective capacities that are affected in autism.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that abnormal processing of multiple sensory modalities on subsecond time scales might impede the acquisition of cognitive and affective capacities that are affected in autism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the cited observations.

claim: Abnormal sensory processing in autism is likely to arise in part from genetic mutations and variants that predispose for neural circuit dysfunction.
source: Abnormal sensory processing in autism is likely to arise in part from genetic mutations and variants that predispose for neural circuit dysfunction.
evidence: This is a general statement based on current understanding of autism etiology.

claim: Delay eyeblink conditioning is found in multiple mammalian species.
source: To investigate the ability to associate two near-simultaneous sensory inputs, we used delay eyeblink conditioning, a form of learning that is found in multiple mammalian species (McCormick and Thompson, 1984; Ivarsson and Hesslow, 1994; Boele et al., 2010; Heiney et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Persons with autism show alterations to delay eyeblink conditioning.
source: Persons with autism show alterations to delay eyeblink conditioning (Sears et al., 1994; Oristaglio et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Delay eyeblink conditioning depends on plasticity in the cerebellum.
source: Delay eyeblink conditioning depends on plasticity in the cerebellum, a common site of anatomical deviation in patients with autism, and cerebellar gross and cellular malformation are common features of autistic brains (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The cerebellum is a common site of anatomical deviation in patients with autism.
source: Delay eyeblink conditioning depends on plasticity in the cerebellum, a common site of anatomical deviation in patients with autism, and cerebellar gross and cellular malformation are common features of autistic brains (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cerebellar gross and cellular malformation are common features of autistic brains.
source: Delay eyeblink conditioning depends on plasticity in the cerebellum, a common site of anatomical deviation in patients with autism, and cerebellar gross and cellular malformation are common features of autistic brains (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Autism is among the most heritable of neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Autism is among the most heritable of neuropsychiatric disorders (Gaugler et al., 2014), and hundreds of autism risk loci have been identified (Abrahams and Geschwind, 2008; Devlin and Scherer, 2012; Stein et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Hundreds of autism risk loci have been identified.
source: Autism is among the most heritable of neuropsychiatric disorders (Gaugler et al., 2014), and hundreds of autism risk loci have been identified (Abrahams and Geschwind, 2008; Devlin and Scherer, 2012; Stein et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Shank3+/ΔC is a C-terminal deletion model of Shank3 associated with Phelan-McDermid syndrome.
source: Four of the models incorporate global mutations with strong expression in the cerebellum: Shank3+/ΔC, the C-terminal deletion model of Shank3 associated with Phelan-McDermid syndrome (Kouser et al., 2011, 2013); Mecp2R308/Y, a mild truncation model of Mecp2 associated with Rett syndrome (Ben-Shachar et al., 2009; Shahbazian et al., 2002a; Moretti et al., 2006; De Filippis et al., 2010); Cntnap2−/−, a knockout of Cntnap2 associated with cortical dysplasia-focal epilepsy syndrome (Peñagarikano et al., 2011); and patDp/+, a mouse model of the 15q(11–13) duplication syndrome closely linked to autism (Nakatani et al., 2009; Tamada et al., 2010; Piochon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mecp2R308/Y is a mild truncation model of Mecp2 associated with Rett syndrome.
source: Four of the models incorporate global mutations with strong expression in the cerebellum: Shank3+/ΔC, the C-terminal deletion model of Shank3 associated with Phelan-McDermid syndrome (Kouser et al., 2011, 2013); Mecp2R308/Y, a mild truncation model of Mecp2 associated with Rett syndrome (Ben-Shachar et al., 2009; Shahbazian et al., 2002a; Moretti et al., 2006; De Filippis et al., 2010); Cntnap2−/−, a knockout of Cntnap2 associated with cortical dysplasia-focal epilepsy syndrome (Peñagarikano et al., 2011); and patDp/+, a mouse model of the 15q(11–13) duplication syndrome closely linked to autism (Nakatani et al., 2009; Tamada et al., 2010; Piochon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cntnap2−/− is a knockout of Cntnap2 associated with cortical dysplasia-focal epilepsy syndrome.
source: Four of the models incorporate global mutations with strong expression in the cerebellum: Shank3+/ΔC, the C-terminal deletion model of Shank3 associated with Phelan-McDermid syndrome (Kouser et al., 2011, 2013); Mecp2R308/Y, a mild truncation model of Mecp2 associated with Rett syndrome (Ben-Shachar et al., 2009; Shahbazian et al., 2002a; Moretti et al., 2006; De Filippis et al., 2010); Cntnap2−/−, a knockout of Cntnap2 associated with cortical dysplasia-focal epilepsy syndrome (Peñagarikano et al., 2011); and patDp/+, a mouse model of the 15q(11–13) duplication syndrome closely linked to autism (Nakatani et al., 2009; Tamada et al., 2010; Piochon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: patDp/+ is a mouse model of the 15q(11–13) duplication syndrome closely linked to autism.
source: Four of the models incorporate global mutations with strong expression in the cerebellum: Shank3+/ΔC, the C-terminal deletion model of Shank3 associated with Phelan-McDermid syndrome (Kouser et al., 2011, 2013); Mecp2R308/Y, a mild truncation model of Mecp2 associated with Rett syndrome (Ben-Shachar et al., 2009; Shahbazian et al., 2002a; Moretti et al., 2006; De Filippis et al., 2010); Cntnap2−/−, a knockout of Cntnap2 associated with cortical dysplasia-focal epilepsy syndrome (Peñagarikano et al., 2011); and patDp/+, a mouse model of the 15q(11–13) duplication syndrome closely linked to autism (Nakatani et al., 2009; Tamada et al., 2010; Piochon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: L7-Tsc1 is a knockout of the tuberous sclerosis protein that specifically affects cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: A fifth model, a knockout of the tuberous sclerosis protein L7-Tsc1 (L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ and L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/flox), specifically affects cerebellar Purkinje cells (PCs) (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: All five mouse models examined in this study have previously shown face validity for autism.
source: All five mouse models examined in this study have previously shown face validity for autism (Silverman et al., 2010), with alterations in social behavior, ultrasonic vocalization, and repetitive behaviors.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The five mouse models show alterations in social behavior, ultrasonic vocalization, and repetitive behaviors.
source: All five mouse models examined in this study have previously shown face validity for autism (Silverman et al., 2010), with alterations in social behavior, ultrasonic vocalization, and repetitive behaviors.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cntnap2−/− mice show enhanced performance on the accelerating rotarod.
source: Cntnap2−/− mice and patDp/+ mice show enhanced performance on a gross motor task, the accelerating rotarod (Nakatani et al., 2009; Peñagarikano et al., 2011); but the other three mouse models do not (Shahbazian et al., 2002a; Kouser et al., 2011; Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: patDp/+ mice show enhanced performance on the accelerating rotarod.
source: Cntnap2−/− mice and patDp/+ mice show enhanced performance on a gross motor task, the accelerating rotarod (Nakatani et al., 2009; Peñagarikano et al., 2011); but the other three mouse models do not (Shahbazian et al., 2002a; Kouser et al., 2011; Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Shank3+/ΔC, Mecp2R308/Y, and L7-Tsc1 mice do not show enhanced performance on the accelerating rotarod.
source: Cntnap2−/− mice and patDp/+ mice show enhanced performance on a gross motor task, the accelerating rotarod (Nakatani et al., 2009; Peñagarikano et al., 2011); but the other three mouse models do not (Shahbazian et al., 2002a; Kouser et al., 2011; Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: patDp/+ mice have alterations in gait.
source: In addition, patDp/+ has been tested and shown to have alterations in gait (Piochon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Over the course of training with a light-flash conditioned stimulus and a co-terminating corneal-airpuff unconditioned stimulus, a conditioned response developed with a gradually rising time course that peaked at the time of the US onset.
source: Over the course of training with a light-flash conditioned stimulus (CS; ultraviolet LED, 280 ms) and a co-terminating corneal-airpuff unconditioned stimulus (US; 30 ms), a conditioned response (CR) developed with a gradually rising time course that peaked at the time of the US onset (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Extinction consisted of 110 trials of CS-only trials and 110 trials of US-only trials over four daily sessions and led to the near-disappearance of the CR.
source: Extinction consisted of 110 trials of CS-only trials and 110 trials of US-only trials over four daily sessions and led to the near-disappearance of the CR (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Three sessions of reacquisition resulted in a rapid return of the CR.
source: Three sessions of reacquisition (identical to acquisition) resulted in a rapid return of the CR (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There was no significant difference among wild-type cohorts in any learning parameter.
source: We found no significant difference among wild-type cohorts in any learning parameter.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: There were no statistically significant differences in time course of extinction or reacquisition among wild-type cohorts.
source: In addition, we did not find statistically significant differences in time course of extinction or reacquisition.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice reached a response probability of 32.0 ± 4.3%, significantly lower than the 51.5 ± 3.5% level reached in control littermates.
source: In L7-Tsc1 mice (Figure 3A), heterozygous mutant mice (L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+or HET, n = 18) reached a response probability of 32.0 ± 4.3%, significantly lower than the 51.5 ± 3.5% level reached in control littermates (n = 16) (last four training sessions; unpaired two-sample t-test, p = 0.01; effect size, Cohen's d′ = 1.21).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/flox mice completely failed to acquire CRs.
source: Furthermore, homozygous mutant mice (L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ or MUT, n = 5) completely failed to acquire CRs (1.4% ± 0.7% in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/flox, n = 5; one-way analysis of variance test (ANOVA) across all groups, p < 0.0001, F(2,35) = 19.82, with Bonferroni post hoc statistical differences between L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/flox and wild-type littermates, p = 3 × 10−9, Cohen's d′ = 3.01, and L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ and wild-type littermates, p = 0.00002, d′ = 1.41).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Cntnap2−/− mice reached a response probability of 35.1% ± 6.2%, significantly lower than the 57.2% ± 2.9% level reached in wild-type littermates.
source: In Cntnap2 mice (Figure 3B), homozygous mutant mice (Cntnap2−/−, n = 12) reached a response probability of 35.1% ± 6.2%, significantly lower than the 57.2% ± 2.9% level reached in wild-type littermates (Cntnap2+/+, n = 13) (last four training sessions; Bonferroni post hoc test after one-way ANOVA, p = 0.007, d′ = 0.96).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Cntnap2+/− mice were statistically indistinguishable in learning or response amplitude from wild-type mice.
source: Notably, Cntnap2+/− mice, which show behavioral similarity to Cntnap2+/+ mice (Peñagarikano et al., 2011), were likewise statistically indistinguishable in learning or response amplitude from wild-type mice (n = 14 mice; Bonferroni post hoc tests after one-way ANOVA, p > 0.5).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: Shank3+/ΔC mice reached a response probability of 55.9% ± 3.7%, lower than the 67.2% ± 2.2% reached in the wild-type littermates.
source: In Shank3ΔC mice (Figure 3C), the heterozygous mutant mice (Shank3+/ΔC, n = 17) reached a response probability of 55.9% ± 3.7%, lower than the 67.2% ± 2.2% reached in the wild-type littermates (Shank3+/+, n = 21) (unpaired two-sample t-test, p = 0.015, d′ = 1.10).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In L7-Tsc1, Cntnap2, and Shank3ΔC mice, probability deficits were present throughout training.
source: In all three mouse models, probability deficits were present throughout training (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, main genotype effect; Cntnap2−/−: F(1,23) = 7.72, p = 0.01; L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/flox: F(1,23) = 11.70, p = 0.002; Shank3+/ΔC: F(1,25) = 4.59, p = 0.04).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Mecp2R308/Y heterozygotes did not show differences in learning probability or time course.
source: One model did not show differences in learning probability or time course: Mecp2R308/Y heterozygotes (Figure 3D; 57.2% ± 2.9% WT vs 57.8% ± 3.6% Mecp2R308/Y, unpaired two-sample t-test, p = 0.9; two-way repeated measures ANOVA: main genotype effect, F(1,22) = 0.10, p = 0.7).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Response probability in patDp/+ mice was smaller than wild-type littermates throughout acquisition training.
source: Throughout acquisition training, response probability in patDp/+ mice (n = 10) was smaller than wild-type littermates (n = 11) (two-way repeated measures ANOVA: main genotype effect, F(1,19) = 19.84, p = 0.0003), culminating in a difference at the end of training (34.2% ± 2.9% patDp/+ vs, 49.2% ± 2.6% WT, unpaired two-sample t-test, p = 0.001, d′ = 1.46).
evidence: This is a finding from re-analysis of previously published data with statistical analysis.

claim: L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice generated smaller-amplitude learned blinks throughout training.
source: L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice generated smaller-amplitude learned blinks throughout training (two-way repeated measures ANOVA: main genotype effect, F(1,23) = 7.71 p = 0.01) that culminated in a difference in amplitude at the end of training (last four training sessions: 0.28 ± 0.03 in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ vs 0.39 ± 0.05 in littermate controls, unpaired two-sample t-test, p = 0.02, d′ = 0.86) (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In Shank3ΔC mice, response amplitude was similar to wild-type for most of training, but culminated in a small reduction by the end of training.
source: In Shank3ΔC mice (Figure 4C), response amplitude was similar to wild-type for most of training (main genotype effect, F(1,24) = 1.45, p = 0.2), but culminated in a small reduction by the end of training (0.31 ± 0.02 Shank3+/ΔC vs 0.36 ± 0.01 Shank3+/+, p = 0.03, d′ = 0.38).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Mecp2R308/Y mice showed consistently smaller learned responses throughout training.
source: Mecp2R308/Y mice (Figure 4D; n = 11) showed consistently smaller learned responses throughout training (two-way repeated measures ANOVA: main genotype effect: F(1,22) = 12.72, p = 0.002), culminating in a difference in amplitude at the end of training (last four training sessions, 0.28 ± 0.02 Mecp2R308/Y in vs 0.44 ± 0.04 WT, unpaired two-sample t-test, p = 0.002, d′ = 1.11).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: CRs in Mecp2R308/Y mice reached maximum amplitude much earlier in the training period.
source: CRs in Mecp2R308/Y mice also reached maximum amplitude much earlier in the training period (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No statistically significant differences in response amplitude or its development were observed in Cntnap2 mice.
source: We did not observe statistically significant differences in response amplitude or its development in Cntnap2 mice (two-way repeated measures ANOVA: main genotype effect, F(2,32) = 0.15, p = 0.85; 0.32 ± 0.03 Cntnap2−/− vs 0.34 ± 0.02 Cntnap2+/+, Bonferroni post hoc test after one-way ANOVA, p = 0.82) (Figure 4B, right) or in 15q duplication mice (two-way repeated measures ANOVA: main genotype effect, F(1,19) = 1.81, p = 0.2), including at the end of training (last four training sessions 0.31 ± 0.02 WT vs 0.27 ± 0.05 patDp/+, unpaired two-sample t-test, p = 0.4; also see Piochon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: No statistically significant differences in response amplitude or its development were observed in 15q duplication mice.
source: We did not observe statistically significant differences in response amplitude or its development in Cntnap2 mice (two-way repeated measures ANOVA: main genotype effect, F(2,32) = 0.15, p = 0.85; 0.32 ± 0.03 Cntnap2−/− vs 0.34 ± 0.02 Cntnap2+/+, Bonferroni post hoc test after one-way ANOVA, p = 0.82) (Figure 4B, right) or in 15q duplication mice (two-way repeated measures ANOVA: main genotype effect, F(1,19) = 1.81, p = 0.2), including at the end of training (last four training sessions 0.31 ± 0.02 WT vs 0.27 ± 0.05 patDp/+, unpaired two-sample t-test, p = 0.4; also see Piochon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: After training, 4 days of extinction led to the near-disappearance of CRs in all autism model groups except for L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/flox.
source: After training, 4 days of extinction led to the near-disappearance of CRs in all autism model groups (CR percentage, day 12 acquisition vs day 4 extinction; paired t-tests, p < 0.05 for all comparisons) except for L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/flox, which did not acquire CRs in the first place.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The time courses of extinction were not statistically distinguishable between any autism model group and its corresponding wild-type littermates.
source: The time courses of extinction were not statistically distinguishable between any autism model group and its corresponding wild-type littermates (p > 0.05 for all main genotype effects), indicating that perturbation of cerebellar cortex-dependent and other mechanisms that are necessary for initial eyeblink conditioning (Robleto et al., 2004) did not strongly affect overall extinction in the mouse models.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: The mouse models that initially acquired CRs successfully reacquired CRs after 3 days of retraining.
source: In addition, the mouse models that initially acquired CRs also successfully reacquired CRs after 3 days of retraining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; paired t-tests of day 4 extinction vs day 3 reacquisition, p < 0.05 for all comparisons), with no appreciable difference in CR percentage between groups (p > 0.05 for all instances).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Savings is thought to depend in part on plasticity in the DCN.
source: The accelerated nature of this reacquisition, a process known as savings, is thought to depend in part on plasticity in the DCN (Medina et al., 2001; Ohyama et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Learning deficits in the mouse models tested were specific to acquisition and were not observed in extinction or reacquisition.
source: In short, learning deficits in the mouse models tested were specific to acquisition and were not observed in extinction or reacquisition.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Learned responses produced by the Shank3+/ΔC mice began at the same time as wild-type littermates.

evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Learned responses produced by the Shank3+/ΔC mice rose faster than wild-type littermates.
source: Learned responses produced by the Shank3+/ΔC mice began at the same time (onset latency: 148.7 ± 4.9 ms Shank3+/+, vs 144.6 ± 4.4 ms Shank3+/ΔC, p = 0.5), rose faster (rise time: 91.8 ± 0.5 ms Shank3+/+ vs 79.5 ± 0.3 ms Shank3+/ΔC, p = 0.04, d′ = 0.70), and peaked earlier (peak latency: 317.5 ± 9.0 ms Shank3+/+ vs 287.7 ± 5.8 ms Shank3+/ΔC, p = 0.03, d′ = 1.02) (Figure 5A, right) compared to wild-type littermates.

claim: In Mecp2R308/Y animals, learned responses began at the same time as wild-type littermates.

claim: In Mecp2R308/Y animals, learned responses rose more slowly than wild-type littermates.
source: In Mecp2R308/Y animals, learned responses began at the same time (onset latency: 120.9 ± 4.0 ms WT vs 117.7 ± 4.9 ms Mecp2R308/Y, p = 0.6), rose more slowly (rise time: 113.2 ± 12.4 ms WT vs 158.4 ± 15.6 ms Mecp2R308/Y, p = 0.04, d′ = 1.04), and peaked later (peak latency: 278.3 ± 14.9 ms WT vs 328.8 ± 16.4 ms Mecp2R308/Y, p = 0.04, d′ = 1.03) compared with wild-type littermates (Figure 5B, right).

claim: In Mecp2R308/Y animals, learned responses peaked later than wild-type littermates.

evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: No alterations in onset latency, peak latency, or rise time could be detected in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice.
source: No alterations in onset latency, peak latency, or rise time could be detected in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ (Figure 5C), Cntnap2−/− mice (Figure 5D), or patDp/+ mice (Piochon et al., 2014) (p > 0.05 for all comparisons; summary of all mouse lines, Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: No alterations in onset latency, peak latency, or rise time could be detected in Cntnap2−/− mice.
source: No alterations in onset latency, peak latency, or rise time could be detected in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ (Figure 5C), Cntnap2−/− mice (Figure 5D), or patDp/+ mice (Piochon et al., 2014) (p > 0.05 for all comparisons; summary of all mouse lines, Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: No alterations in onset latency, peak latency, or rise time could be detected in patDp/+ mice.
source: No alterations in onset latency, peak latency, or rise time could be detected in L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ (Figure 5C), Cntnap2−/− mice (Figure 5D), or patDp/+ mice (Piochon et al., 2014) (p > 0.05 for all comparisons; summary of all mouse lines, Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: No differences in unconditioned response latency measured from US onset were found in any of the five mouse models.
source: In US-only trials, we found no differences in unconditioned response (UR) latency measured from US onset (p ≥ 0.2 for unpaired comparisons for each cohort) or UR rise time (p ≥ 0.4 for unpaired two-sample comparisons for each cohort) (Table 1, 'Unconditioned response') and no differences in the correlation between UR velocity and UR magnitude (analysis of covariance group × peak interaction, p ≥ 0.2 for all cohorts).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: No differences in unconditioned response rise time were found in any of the five mouse models.
source: In US-only trials, we found no differences in unconditioned response (UR) latency measured from US onset (p ≥ 0.2 for unpaired comparisons for each cohort) or UR rise time (p ≥ 0.4 for unpaired two-sample comparisons for each cohort) (Table 1, 'Unconditioned response') and no differences in the correlation between UR velocity and UR magnitude (analysis of covariance group × peak interaction, p ≥ 0.2 for all cohorts).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: No differences in the correlation between UR velocity and UR magnitude were found in any of the five mouse models.
source: In US-only trials, we found no differences in unconditioned response (UR) latency measured from US onset (p ≥ 0.2 for unpaired comparisons for each cohort) or UR rise time (p ≥ 0.4 for unpaired two-sample comparisons for each cohort) (Table 1, 'Unconditioned response') and no differences in the correlation between UR velocity and UR magnitude (analysis of covariance group × peak interaction, p ≥ 0.2 for all cohorts).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: No differences among wild-type cohorts were detected for UR latency.
source: We detected no differences among wild-type cohorts for UR latency (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.5, F(4,64) = 0.92) or velocity (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.4, F(4,64) = 1.08).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: No differences among wild-type cohorts were detected for UR velocity.
source: We detected no differences among wild-type cohorts for UR latency (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.5, F(4,64) = 0.92) or velocity (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.4, F(4,64) = 1.08).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Eyelid opening occurred on a similar fraction of trials in all groups.
source: Eyelid opening only occurred when animals had not yet begun to produce CRs, indicating that these responses were non-associative in nature. Eyelid opening occurred on a similar fraction of trials in all groups (p > 0.1 for unpaired comparisons between each autism model and wild-type littermates).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Wild-type groups did not differ detectably in eyelid opening.
source: Wild-type groups also did not differ detectably (one-way ANOVA, p = 0.9, F(4,64) = 0.22).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Sensory sensitivity was unaltered in any of the mouse models.
source: In summary, sensory sensitivity was unaltered in any of the mouse models, and thus, deficits in delay eyeblink conditioning were not accompanied by upstream alterations in sensory sensitivity or downstream deficits in blink capability.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Deficits in delay eyeblink conditioning were not accompanied by upstream alterations in sensory sensitivity or downstream deficits in blink capability.
source: In summary, sensory sensitivity was unaltered in any of the mouse models, and thus, deficits in delay eyeblink conditioning were not accompanied by upstream alterations in sensory sensitivity or downstream deficits in blink capability.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: No differences between mutant and wild-type mice in forepaw stance, forepaw stride, hindpaw stance, and hindpaw stride were observed in Cntnap2−/− mice, L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice, and Shank3+/ΔC mice.
source: We measured forepaw stance, forepaw stride, hindpaw stance, and hindpaw stride. We observed no differences between mutant and wild-type mice in Cntnap2−/− mice, L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice, and Shank3+/ΔC mice (two-sample t-test, p > 0.05 for all comparisons; Table 1, 'Gait analysis').
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ result is consistent with previous reports.
source: The L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ result is consistent with previous reports (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Gross motor function in adult ASD mouse models is not a necessary consequence of disruption in cerebellum-dependent learning.
source: Taken together with past research, our findings indicate that gross motor function in adult ASD mouse models is not a necessary consequence of disruption in cerebellum-dependent learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and previous research.

claim: After four training sessions, no statistically detectable difference in the ability to find the platform in a water Y-maze was observed in Cntnap2−/− mice, L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice, or Shank3+/ΔC mice.
source: After four training sessions, we did not observe any statistically detectable difference in the ability to find the platform in Cntnap2−/− mice, L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice, or Shank3+/ΔC mice (two-sample t-test, p > 0.05 for all comparisons; Table 1, 'Swimming Y-maze acquisition').
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ finding is consistent with previous reports of normal T-maze acquisition.
source: The L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ finding is consistent with previous reports of normal T-maze acquisition (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The eyeblink-conditioning deficits observed do not reflect a broad impairment in learning mechanisms.
source: Therefore, the eyeblink-conditioning deficits we have observed do not reflect a broad impairment in learning mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In Shank3+/ΔC, Cntnap2−/−, Mecp2R308/Y, and patDp/+ mice, no differences between mutant mice and wild-type littermates in PC density, anterior or posterior granule layer thickness, and anterior or posterior molecular layer thickness were found.
source: Using histological methods, in Shank3+/ΔC, Cntnap2−/−, Mecp2R308/Y, and patDp/+ mice, we found no differences between mutant mice and wild-type littermates in PC density, anterior or posterior granule layer thickness, and anterior or posterior molecular layer thickness (p > 0.1, all comparisons).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice, no difference for anterior or posterior granule layer thickness and molecular layer thickness was found.
source: In L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice, for which alterations in PC density have been previously reported (Tsai et al., 2012), we found no difference for anterior or posterior granule layer thickness and molecular layer thickness for L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ (p > 0.1, all comparisons).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: With the exception of L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice, these mouse lines do not show gross alterations in granule or PC density.
source: In summary, with the exception of L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice, these mouse lines do not show gross alterations in granule or PC density.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Only Shank3+/ΔC mice differed from wild type in Sholl analysis, showing higher complexity of distal dendrites.
source: Only Shank3+/ΔC mice differed from wild type, showing higher complexity of distal dendrites (two-way repeated measures ANOVA, main genotype effect, F(1,39) = 3.50, p = 0.07), with a significant distance × genotype interaction (F(16,624) = 2.77, p = 0.0002; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In Shank3+/ΔC mice, the center of mass of the Sholl distribution was farther from the soma compared with wild type.
source: Further analysis of Shank3+/ΔC mice revealed that compared with wild type, the center of mass of the Sholl distribution was farther from the soma (p = 0.03) and had a greater total number of crossings at distances farther than 96 μm from the soma (p = 0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: In Shank3+/ΔC mice, there was a greater total number of crossings at distances farther than 96 μm from the soma compared with wild type.
source: Further analysis of Shank3+/ΔC mice revealed that compared with wild type, the center of mass of the Sholl distribution was farther from the soma (p = 0.03) and had a greater total number of crossings at distances farther than 96 μm from the soma (p = 0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: A decrease in the number of visible spines per 10 μm on distal dendrites was found in Shank3+/ΔC mice.
source: Closer examination of PC arbors (Figure 6B) revealed a decrease in the number of visible spines per 10 μm on distal dendrites of Shank3+/ΔC mice (p = 0.04) and Mecp2R308/Y mice (p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: A decrease in the number of visible spines per 10 μm on distal dendrites was found in Mecp2R308/Y mice.
source: Closer examination of PC arbors (Figure 6B) revealed a decrease in the number of visible spines per 10 μm on distal dendrites of Shank3+/ΔC mice (p = 0.04) and Mecp2R308/Y mice (p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The remaining three models showed no differences in either PC arbors or spine density.
source: The remaining three models showed no differences in either PC arbors or spine density (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1; p > 0.3 for main group effect and p > 0.5 for space × genotype interactions for all comparisons; p > 0.4 for all pairwise comparisons of spine density).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Differences in dendritic morphology were found specifically in Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y mice, consistent with alterations in GrC input and/or PC dendritic growth mechanisms.
source: In summary, differences in dendritic morphology were found specifically in Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y mice, consistent with alterations in GrC input and/or PC dendritic growth mechanisms.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data with interpretation.

claim: Five mouse models of ASD show deficits in delay eyeblink conditioning.
source: Our principal finding is that five mouse models of ASD show deficits in delay eyeblink conditioning, a learning task that requires the cerebellum (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Delay eyeblink conditioning is a learning task that requires the cerebellum.
source: Our principal finding is that five mouse models of ASD show deficits in delay eyeblink conditioning, a learning task that requires the cerebellum (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about delay eyeblink conditioning.

claim: The five models tested showed three major categories of deficit: in the process of acquiring the CR, in the amplitude of the CR, and in the timing of the CR.
source: The five models tested showed three major categories of deficit (Figure 7B): in the process of acquiring the CR, in the amplitude of the CR, and in the timing of the CR.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Defects in the reliable learning and production of CRs might be interpreted as disruption of the olivocerebellar 'instruction' system.
source: Thus, defects in the reliable learning and production of CRs might be interpreted as disruption of the olivocerebellar 'instruction' system (Garcia et al., 1999) or the granule cell layer 'representation' system (Arenz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on known cerebellar circuitry and citations to previous research.

claim: Defects in the reliable learning and production of CRs might be interpreted as disruption of the granule cell layer 'representation' system.
source: Thus, defects in the reliable learning and production of CRs might be interpreted as disruption of the olivocerebellar 'instruction' system (Garcia et al., 1999) or the granule cell layer 'representation' system (Arenz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on known cerebellar circuitry and citations to previous research.

claim: Activity in the GrC network is thought to represent key temporal components to drive a well-timed response.
source: Activity in the GrC network, which receives direct mf input, is thought to represent key temporal components to drive a well-timed response (Medina and Mauk, 2000; D'Angelo and De Zeeuw, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PC sodium-based simple-spike output acts as an approximately linear readout of synaptic drive.
source: Because PC sodium-based simple-spike output acts as an approximately linear readout of synaptic drive (Walter and Khodakhah, 2006), the time course of CR production might be expected to be constructed from summed patterns of activity in specific combinations of GrCs and inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Defects in response timing and amplitude might be interpreted as disruption of synaptic transmission and/or plasticity in the MF pathway.
source: Therefore, defects in response timing and amplitude might be interpreted as disruption of synaptic transmission and/or plasticity in the MF pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on known cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Four mouse models showed decreases in the CR probability: L7-Tsc1, patDp/+, Cntnap2−/−, and Shank3+/ΔC.
source: Four mouse models showed decreases in the CR probability: L7-Tsc1 (L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ and L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/flox), patDp/+, Cntnap2−/−, and Shank3+/ΔC.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The disrupted genes in three models (L7-Tsc1, patDp/+, and Cntnap2−/−) are expressed in PCs, inferior olive, and/or DCN.
source: Upon investigating patterns of gene expression, we found that the disrupted genes in three models (L7-Tsc1, patDp/+, and Cntnap2−/−) are expressed in PCs, inferior olive, and/or DCN (Figure 7A, light green and red [regular case], respectively; Figure 7C, red).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis.

claim: In L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice, early-life loss of Tsc1 leads to increased spine density and decreased excitability in PCs.
source: In L7/Pcp2Cre::Tsc1flox/+ mice, which are PC-specific, early-life loss of Tsc1 leads to increased spine density and decreased excitability in PCs (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Decreased excitability in PCs can affect learning by interfering with climbing fiber-based instruction.
source: This decreased excitability can affect learning by interfering with climbing fiber (cf)-based instruction, either by reducing PC dendritic excitability or by making the cerebellar cortex less effective at influencing the DCN, resulting in inhibited IO responsiveness to the US (Schonewille et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on known cerebellar circuitry and citation to previous research.

claim: patDp/+ mice show cf structural plasticity during development and deregulated PF-PC LTD in adults.
source: Similarly, patDp/+ mice show cf structural plasticity during development and deregulated PF-PC LTD in adults (Piochon et al., 2014), echoing findings in other models (Koekkoek et al., 2005; Baudouin et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Other forms of cerebellar plasticity can contribute to learning in the absence of PF-PC LTD.
source: It should be noted that other forms of cerebellar plasticity can contribute to learning in the absence of PF-PC LTD (Schonewille et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cerebellar learning defects in autism mouse models may be strongly shaped by reduced function in the olivocerebellar circuit and associated synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
source: Taken together, the evidence suggests that cerebellar learning defects in autism mouse models may be strongly shaped by reduced function in the olivocerebellar circuit and associated synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and previous research.

claim: Shank3 is expressed specifically at postsynaptic densities in the granule cell layer in the mouse cerebellum.
source: Shank3 is expressed specifically at postsynaptic densities in the granule cell layer in the mouse cerebellum (Tu et al., 1999; Böckers et al., 2004, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurotrophin-3 (NT-3) from GrCs is required for PC dendritic morphogenesis.
source: Neurotrophin-3 (NT-3) from GrCs is required for PC dendritic morphogenesis (Joo et al., 2014), suggesting the possibility that the Shank3+/ΔC mutation may disrupt PC dendritic function.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The Shank3+/ΔC mutation may disrupt PC dendritic function.
source: Neurotrophin-3 (NT-3) from GrCs is required for PC dendritic morphogenesis (Joo et al., 2014), suggesting the possibility that the Shank3+/ΔC mutation may disrupt PC dendritic function.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data and previous research.

claim: Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y genes are expressed in GrCs.
source: We observed both amplitude and timing defects in two mouse models (Figure 7B, gray circles), Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y. These genes are expressed in GrCs (Figure 7A, yellow and turquoise cells, respectively), and Mecp2 is also expressed in Golgi cells (GoCs).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis.

claim: Mecp2 is also expressed in Golgi cells.
source: We observed both amplitude and timing defects in two mouse models (Figure 7B, gray circles), Shank3+/ΔC and Mecp2R308/Y. These genes are expressed in GrCs (Figure 7A, yellow and turquoise cells, respectively), and Mecp2 is also expressed in Golgi cells (GoCs).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis.

claim: Shank3 encodes a scaffolding protein that may influence MF-GrC and GrC-PC synaptic function by reducing glutamatergic transmission and plasticity.
source: Shank3 encodes a scaffolding protein that may influence MF-GrC and GrC-PC synaptic function by reducing glutamatergic transmission and plasticity (e.g., Peça et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2012; Kouser et al., 2013), thus, impairing cerebellar learning (Giza et al., 2010; Andreescu et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mecp2 expression is dramatically upregulated in GrCs after P21, a time when MF-GrC and PF-PC synapses are formed and still maturing.
source: Likewise, Mecp2 expression is dramatically upregulated in GrCs after P21, a time when MF-GrC and PF-PC synapses are formed and still maturing (Altman, 1972), suggesting that Mecp2 plays a role in MF-GrC synapse function (Mullaney et al., 2004) and glutamatergic synaptic transmission and plasticity (Moretti et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Despite the fact that Mecp2 is also expressed in PCs, Mecp2R308/Y mice showed no defect in probability of learning.
source: It is notable that despite the fact that Mecp2 is also expressed in PCs (Mullaney et al., 2004), Mecp2R308/Y mice showed no defect in probability of learning.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with citation to previous research.

claim: Other Mecp2 mutants might show more of a probability phenotype.
source: We chose these mice for their relatively weak motor dysfunction so that we could characterize eyeblink-conditioning deficits in detail. Other Mecp2 mutants might show more of a probability phenotype.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential findings in other models.

claim: Delay eyeblink conditioning depends on processing outside the cerebellum.
source: In addition to specific cerebellar substrates, delay eyeblink conditioning also depends on processing outside the cerebellum (Boele et al., 2010; Figure 7A, dark gray cells; Figure 7C, dark gray arrows).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Several genes in the mouse models (though not Shank3) are likely to be expressed in trigeminal nucleus, red nucleus, and facial nucleus.
source: Several genes in our mouse models (though not Shank3) are likely to be expressed in trigeminal nucleus, which transmits sensory information to the pons and mf pathway, as well as the red nucleus and facial nucleus, which ultimately drive the production of the eyeblink (Figure 7A, dark gray cells; Figure 7C, dark gray arrows; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis.

claim: The acquisition of delay eyeblink conditioning may be modulated by the amygdala and hippocampus.
source: The acquisition of delay eyeblink conditioning may also be modulated by the amygdala and hippocampus (Lee and Kim et al., 2004; Boele et al., 2010; Sakamoto and Endo, 2010; Taub and Mintz, 2010), but we did not detect two known consequences of such modulation, learning during the first training session and short-latency alpha responses to the CS.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research, and the authors report not detecting certain consequences.

claim: Past investigations of autism have reported the percentage of CS-responses that exceed a fixed threshold ('% CRs'), as well as CR size averaged across all trials.
source: Past investigations of autism (Sears et al., 1994; Oristaglio et al., 2013) and Fragile X syndrome (Koekkoek et al., 2005; Tobia and Woodruff-Pak, 2009) have reported the percentage of CS-responses that exceed a fixed threshold ('% CRs'), as well as CR size averaged across all trials.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: These measures conflate changes in the probability of learning with changes in the amplitude of learned responses.
source: However, these measures conflate changes in the probability of learning with changes in the amplitude of learned responses.
evidence: This is a critique of previous methods based on the authors' analysis approach.

claim: In high-functioning autistics, the %CR fraction rose more rapidly than in controls, reaching close to a half-maximum after only two blocks of trials.
source: For example, a study that examined de novo (i.e., no previous conditioning) delay eyeblink conditioning (Sears et al., 1994) found that in high-functioning (average IQ > 100) autistics, the %CR fraction rose more rapidly than in controls, reaching close to a half-maximum after only two blocks of trials.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Impairments in delay eyeblink conditioning have been observed in Fragile X patients.
source: In the direction of loss-of-function, impairments in delay eyeblink conditioning have been observed in Fragile X patients (Koekkoek et al., 2005; Tobia and Woodruff-Pak, 2009); in this case, PC-specific knockout of the Fragile X protein Fmr1 in mice was sufficient to cause eyeblink-conditioning defects, suggesting that learning was specifically perturbed.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PC-specific knockout of the Fragile X protein Fmr1 in mice was sufficient to cause eyeblink-conditioning defects.
source: In the direction of loss-of-function, impairments in delay eyeblink conditioning have been observed in Fragile X patients (Koekkoek et al., 2005; Tobia and Woodruff-Pak, 2009); in this case, PC-specific knockout of the Fragile X protein Fmr1 in mice was sufficient to cause eyeblink-conditioning defects, suggesting that learning was specifically perturbed.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In idiopathic autism, CRs came approximately 50 ms earlier, as measured using both the time to CR onset and the time to CR peak.
source: In idiopathic autism (Sears et al., 1994), CRs came approximately 50 ms earlier, as measured using both the time to CR onset and the time to CR peak.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: After two sessions of trace conditioning, delay conditioning initially leads to a decrease in response onset and latency of approximately 50 ms, followed by a convergence toward normal performance as training continues.
source: Similarly, after two sessions of trace conditioning (Oristaglio et al., 2013), delay conditioning initially leads to a decrease in response onset and latency of approximately 50 ms, followed by a convergence toward normal performance as training continues.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Fragile X patients show no differences in timing in early training sessions.
source: In contrast, Fragile X patients show no differences in timing in early training sessions (Koekkoek et al., 2005; Tobia and Woodruff-Pak, 2009), but after average CR amplitude reaches a plateau, the peak latency to CR decreases by approximately 30 ms (Tobia and Woodruff-Pak, 2009).
